summary: Clarifies when a standards track RFC may refer normatively to a document at a lower maturity level, such as an informational RFC. It explains that exceptions to the usual rule are sometimes needed and describes how to handle them.

plainLanguage.summary: A standards-track RFC may sometimes need a required reference to a less mature document. RFC 3967 explains how the IETF discloses and reviews that exception.

questions: can a standards track rfc cite an informational rfc
what is a downward reference in an rfc
when can an rfc cite a lower maturity document
subtitle: The IETF process for openly reviewing a standards document that must rely on a less mature document.

tldr.problem: IETF process normally bars a standards-track document from depending on a document at a lower maturity level. Some necessary protocols, algorithms, or migration targets exist only in lower-level documents.
tldr.mechanism: The need for a downward normative reference must be stated explicitly during the normal IETF Last Call, so the community and IESG can consider it. An Area Director may later waive repeat notices for the same accepted document and version.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3967 provides a limited path for justified exceptions. It is a Best Current Practice updated by RFC 4897 and RFC 8067.

today: RFC 3967 is a Best Current Practice published in December 2004. It has been updated by RFC 4897 and RFC 8067, and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Rule for Lower-Level References
sections.content:
RFC 2026 says standards-track documents normally must not depend on standards-track documents at a lower maturity level or on non-standards documents, except specifications from other standards bodies. One reason is to avoid making a standard appear more mature than it is. Best Current Practice documents are generally treated like standards-track documents for this rule.

RFC 3967 clarifies how to handle exceptions when a standards-track or BCP document needs a normative reference to a lower-level document.
sections.plainLanguage: A standard normally should not depend on a less mature document. This rule helps readers judge how complete and stable the standard is.

sections.title: What Makes a Reference Normative
sections.content:
A normative reference points to material needed to understand or implement an RFC, or material whose contents effectively form part of that RFC. An informative reference gives background only. The RFC notes that the distinction can be difficult in practice and depends on the document's purpose.

If an implementer needs a packet format or required algorithm defined elsewhere, that reference is normative. An example of one possible algorithm may be informative when the implementer could choose another.
sections.plainLanguage: A reference is normative when an implementer must use the other document to complete the work. A reference that only offers background is informative.

sections.title: Why an Exception May Be Needed
sections.content:
A standards document may need a lower-level reference when an IETF document describes an external protocol or algorithm, when the reference is to a proprietary protocol, or when a migration plan must cover a historic or non-standard protocol. Exceptional legal or procedural reasons can also limit the target document's status. A BCP may need to describe practices for experimental or informational specifications.

Allowing a reference does not remove the IETF's responsibility to make the standard clear enough for interoperable implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes required technical details exist only in a lower-level document. A migration standard may also need to explain how to work with an older protocol.

sections.title: The Last Call Review
sections.content:
When a Standards Track or BCP document needs a normative reference to a lower-maturity document, the normal IETF Last Call must explicitly identify the need for that reference. The IESG considers community comments about whether the reference is appropriate as part of its deliberation.

After the community has accepted a reference to a specific document, an Area Director may waive a notice in later Last Calls. This applies only to the same document and version, and only when the Area Director believes its use is accepted in that technical area. The process should not replace moving a document to the appropriate category when that step is feasible.
sections.plainLanguage: The Last Call must tell the community why the standards document depends on the lower-level reference. The IESG considers the feedback before deciding whether the exception is appropriate.

sections.title: Limits and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the procedure is not an easy way around normal standards process. It is intended for specific cases where moving the referenced document to the needed category is problematic and unlikely to happen.

The document is not known to create new Internet vulnerabilities. Inappropriate or excessive use could weaken the quality of standards or the rigor of security review, which the RFC describes as a possible downgrade attack.
sections.plainLanguage: This exception is for specific cases, not a shortcut around standards review. Too many exceptions could weaken the review of standards, including security requirements.
